prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned prose and poetry that make memory, the body and dream into an expansive imaginative cosmology

statement.case_for: My view from the opening stage stands after the colleagues' arguments. Cărtărescu's public record points to an unmistakable voice and a formal architecture that holds across decades. Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid build memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation into one imaginative system, and the poetry and essays are part of the same project. This is the kind of sustained, original, intellectually deep work the common criteria ask for. The case rests on how the books are built and on the writing, not on national or political symbolism. The late novels appear to extend the earlier ones rather than repeat them, so the oeuvre reads as mature and not as a single peak. This assessment rests on general public knowledge and not on direct reading.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the claim depends on dense, recursive Romanian prose and long-range structure, which translation may carry only partly. The very long late books may also contain excess or repetition that I cannot confirm. The poetry and early work are less accessible in translation, so the balance between the major novels and the rest of the corpus is hard to judge. If those doubts hold, the case narrows to a few large books. Adonis's case rests on a formal transformation of a whole poetic language, which is arguably a larger kind of achievement if it can be verified.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Adonis first. He sees a poetic project that renewed Arabic verse through myth, fragmentation and argument with the classical tradition, supported by essays on tradition and modernity, with a long-established and mature body of work.
responses.response: I take the formal claim seriously. Renewing the language of a poetic tradition is a weighty achievement under our criteria, and the maturity and timing argument is not in doubt. My hesitation is epistemic, and Olsson names the same limit himself. The claim lies in Arabic prosody and diction, which a non-Arabic reader can judge only through secondary accounts and partial translations. That is why I rank Adonis fourth and not higher. I would want a reader of the Arabic to confirm the poems' lasting force, separate from the poet's influence as a critic and cultural figure. Olsson's own second place for Cărtărescu suggests the two cases may be closer in merit than my ranking implies. I keep Adonis as my first alternative.

responses.point: Carlberg ranks Cărtărescu fourth. She grants the strong voice and the large architecture, but questions whether the late, very long books justify their scale, and notes that the poetry and early work are thinly covered in translation.
responses.response: This is the fairest form of the objection and I share it. I cannot rule out excess or recursion in the late works without closer reading, and I do not want to claim more than I can support. Where I differ is on how the doubt should be weighed. The scale looks like part of the method, with memory and the body built into a cumulative cosmology, and not an incidental weakness. If the committee can establish that the later volumes only repeat the earlier ones, that would weaken my position, and I would then move toward Adonis or Anne Carson. Carlberg's own high ranking of Carson, whose work resists reduction to one form, is a reminder that formal invention can be found in more than one place on this list.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first and Wright second. She stresses the long-built fictional cosmos, but also that the effect depends on prose texture and architecture that translation may only partly convey, and that Wright's smaller number of major novels thins the case for sustained breadth.
responses.response: I agree on the translation caveat and on the sustained-breadth question for Wright. This is why I rank Wright third and not first, even though Carpentaria and The Swan Book are formally ambitious and not merely documentary. The case for Wright rests on a small number of large books, and the quality of her later work is something I cannot verify. For Cărtărescu the evidence is broader, with decades of fiction, poetry and essays pointing the same way. I would add that the Wright case, like the Adonis case, must not be allowed to lean on political or cultural significance to make up for a thinner corpus.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Adonis second, and places Michon third. He admires Michon's stylistic exactness and compression, while noting that the compact corpus may support only a narrower claim of broad significance.
responses.response: I agree that Michon's compressed prose has real formal achievement, and I rank him seventh for reasons close to Sem-Sandberg's own qualification. The scale of the corpus makes a claim of breadth across an oeuvre harder to support. Sem-Sandberg is also candid that Michon's style is partly mediated by translation. I would not set aside the case for concentrated depth over volume, but I think it fits Cărtărescu's wider range of forms better than it fits a smaller body of work.

uncertainties: I have not read the work directly. My assessment of Cărtărescu rests on general public knowledge, and I cannot verify how much of the Romanian prose texture survives in translation.
The relative strength of the poetry, early prose and essays against the major novels is not established, and the late long books may be repetitive or overlong.
I cannot judge Arabic prosody, Chinese prose rhythm or Korean and French registers independently, so comparisons across languages rely heavily on translation and secondary accounts.
The weight of the essays, translations and non-textual projects in the Adonis, Carson and Zurita cases remains an open question for a literary citation.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile shows no connection to any shortlisted writer. My own literary practice and my work on Selma Lagerlöf are context only and are not evidence for any candidate.
